analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin prices in federal health programs at the average of prices in other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee in November 2019, but the committee never acted on it and it died at the end of the 116th Congress without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to set a maximum price for insulin, based on the median price charged for the same products in 11 other developed countries, including Japan, Germany, France, and Canada. The cap would apply to insulin sold through Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, the VA, the federal employee health plan, and Indian Health Service programs — and would also require drugmakers to sell insulin to uninsured and privately insured people at that same price. A company that overcharged would face a civil penalty equal to 10 times its excess revenue, with the money split between Medicare and NIH research. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 7 million Americans who use insulin, especially the millions enrolled in Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, VA care, and Indian Health Service programs, who would have paid no more than an international reference price for insulin, including out-of-pocket costs. Uninsured and privately insured people also benefit, because the bill requires manufacturers to offer insulin at the reference price to everyone, not just federal program enrollees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insulin users in federal health programs

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary of Health and Human Services would set an annual reference price for insulin equal to the median wholesale price in 11 reference countries (Japan, Germany, the UK, France, Italy, Canada, Australia, Spain, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Sweden), and insulin prices in federal health programs — including the cost-sharing patients pay — could not exceed that price [S3].

The cap would cover Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, TRICARE, VA hospital and medical care, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and programs funded under the Indian Health Care Improvement Act [S3].

Manufacturers would have to offer insulin at the reference price to all individuals, including people who are uninsured or covered by private insurance — extending the price cap beyond the federal programs themselves [S3].

A manufacturer that charged above the reference price would face a civil penalty each year equal to 10 times the difference between what it actually received and what it would have received at the reference price; half the money would go to Medicare's trust funds and half to NIH for drug research [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers — primarily the three companies that dominate the U.S. insulin market — would lose the gap between U.S. prices and the lower prices charged in other developed countries, and would face steep civil penalties for overcharging. Shareholders in those companies would absorb reduced profits. To the extent the cap squeezed revenue, there is some risk of reduced investment in new insulin formulations.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps the wholesale (list) price, and critics of international reference pricing generally argue that tying U.S. prices to those in other countries could reduce manufacturers' incentive to invest in new drug formulations or could lead them to delay launching products in the U.S. or reference countries [S3].

The U.S. pays far more for insulin than the reference countries do, so the cut to manufacturer revenue would be substantial — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge, though the bill's penalty mechanism is designed to make compliance cheaper than overcharging [S3].

The bill leaves the details of how prices are set to the Secretary of Health and Human Services, so its real-world effect would have depended heavily on how a future administration defined the reference price [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of Americans who ration or go into debt to buy insulin, the benefit is direct and large: a hard price ceiling pegged to what other developed countries pay, extended even to the uninsured. The cost falls on a small, highly profitable group of insulin manufacturers, though cutting revenue that far could carry some risk of slower investment in next-generation insulin products. On balance, the bill's benefits to patients would likely have outweighed its costs to the industry — which is part of why the industry's allies had reason to see that it never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley, joined by Senator Richard Durbin, introduced the bill on November 7, 2019 [S3].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers, who keep the difference between U.S. insulin prices and the lower prices charged in other developed countries, are better off because the bill never advanced. Nobody else gains from this outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insulin manufacturers keep the price gap

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the bill never advanced far enough for a vote in which partisan lines could be measured; the Senate was controlled by Republicans, whose committee and floor leadership took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would cap what the three dominant insulin makers can charge at the median price in 11 other developed countries — including what patients pay out of pocket — and impose a penalty of 10 times the excess revenue for overcharging. Their interest in keeping U.S. prices, the highest in the reference set, runs directly against insulin users' interest in paying international prices.

The bill is limited to insulin, but it uses international reference pricing — a mechanism the broader brand-name drug industry opposes because it threatens to become a template for capping prices of other drugs. Half of any collected penalties would flow to NIH research, a partial offset.
